extracted.intended_audience: architects, students of architecture, art critics, and educated readers interested in Gothic architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and formative rules for recognizing, designing, and judging Gothic (foliated) architecture — covering structural forms (arches, gables, cusps), ornament (foliation, sculpture), scale considerations, and stylistic distinctions between early and late Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — Foliated Architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: "Foliated Architecture, which uses the pointed arch for the roof proper, and the gable for the roof-mask."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is given as the final, compact definition of Gothic in the text. It functions as the primary test: a building that uses the pointed arch in its roof proper and the gable as its roof-mask qualifies as Gothic/foliated architecture. (See accompanying explanation of terms: roof proper = internal shell/vault/ceiling; roof-mask = external covering/protection.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pointed arch for the roof proper
rubrics_metrics.description: "Gothic architecture is that which uses, if possible, the pointed arch in the roof proper."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible the principal form adopted in the stone vaulting or the timbers of the roof proper should be the pointed arch; this is the first step in defining Gothic. Flat or other ceilings may occur for practical reasons without destroying purity, but the pointed arch is the normative structural form for roofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the gable for the roof-mask (essential, not optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Gothic architecture is that which uses the pointed arch for the roof proper, and the gable for the roof-mask."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The gable as external roof-mask is a far more essential feature than the pointed vault; employing any other conspicuous roof-mask (dome, Turkish, Chinese, etc.) is wilful transgression and corrupts the Gothic character in proportion to its conspicuousness. Domestic buildings may retain Gothic character through bold gables even when other elements (e.g., windows) are square.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothicness is a matter of degree
rubrics_metrics.description: A building is not simply Gothic or not Gothic in form; "we can only say that it is more or less Gothic, in proportion to the number of Gothic forms which it unites."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate by counting and weighing Gothic forms (pointed arches, gables, foliation, tracery, cusps, etc.). Partial presence of Gothic elements confers partial Gothic character; purity depends on how consistently the Gothic group of forms is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundance (accumulation of ornament) as a constituent element
rubrics_metrics.description: REDUNDANCE — the uncalculating bestowal of the wealth of its labor; accumulation of ornament is a part of Gothic humility and appeal to all classes of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richness and ornamental accumulation can be an essential virtue of Gothic architecture: it allows co-operation of many hands, conceals imperfect workmanship, appeals to both rude and refined minds, and expresses devotion and naturalistic sympathy. However, excessive ornament without inventive merit can be commonplace; the best examples balance richness with true invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foliation (essential decorative principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: "No Gothic is either good or characteristic which is not foliated either in its arches or apertures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foliation (cusps, foils, traceries) must appear somewhere in the design—either the bearing arches are foliated or the apertures/traceries are. Tracery originated as penetrations shaped like stars/leaves; good traceries cluster foils with mouldings following their outlines. Absence of foliation indicates an imperfect or uncharacteristic Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid merely imitative or random foliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Foliation is the easiest method of decoration; random crossing lines filled with foils will satisfy most people but lack invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution: unskilled builders can produce superficially 'Gothic' effects by arbitrary foliation patterns. True quality requires invention and skill in floral decoration and moulding disposition; floral/figure ornament demands inventive design rather than random foilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cusps and cusped arch form for strength and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all possible forms of the pointed arch (given a certain weight of material), the form generically represented at e (Fig. XV) is the strongest — achieved by thickening the flanks and adding cusps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cusped/pointed arches (with cusps projecting) combine structural strength and ornament. On small scales, cusps serve structural advantage and beauty; on very large spans heavy cusps are impractical and mass/tracery must provide stability instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale constraint on cusps and foliation
rubrics_metrics.description: The structural advantage of the cusp is available only in arches on a comparatively small scale; very large arches cannot carry heavy cusps, and such arches rely on masonry mass and tracery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing, apply cusped ornament where spans are moderate; for large vaults use massing and tracery to suggest support rather than heavy projecting cusps, which would be insecure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three fundamental roofing/covering forms and corresponding 'pure' architectures
rubrics_metrics.description: There are only three ways of bridging an interval between piers: A, the lintel; B, the round arch; C, the gable — corresponding to Greek (lintel), Romanesque (round arch), and Gothic (gable) architectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite structural taxonomy to classify and judge style and purity: the predominant spanning method determines the architecture's generic family. Varieties and decorations may vary widely, but they are referable back to these three fundamental roofing types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gable steepness test: Gothic vs Romanesque gables
rubrics_metrics.description: A Gothic gable must have all its angles acute; a Romanesque one must have the upper one obtuse. Practical test: strike a semicircle on its base — if the top rises above the semicircle it's Gothic; if it falls beneath, Romanesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this simple geometric rule when distinguishing northern (Gothic, steep) from southern (Romanesque, flat) gable types. Best forms in each group are distinctly steep or distinctly low; transitional/confused examples may occur where arch and gable are mismatched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foliation should be informed by Naturalism, not literal imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Foliation rose from the love of leafage; the arch is not intended to imitate a leaf, but to be invested with the same characters of beauty (curvature, subdivision, radiation) discovered in leaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design foliation by abstracting the 'sources of beauty' from vegetation — consistent curvature and ordered subdivision — rather than by irregular literal copying. Keep outlines regular and consistent with masonry strength; irregularity betrays bad imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between foliation and floral/figure sculpture distinguishes quality and period
rubrics_metrics.description: Two vast Gothic schools: early (noble, inventive) uses foliation moderately and floral/figure sculpture profusely; late (ignoble, uninventive, declining) uses foliation immoderately and subordinates sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess period and quality by how foliation and sculpture are balanced. Early/high Gothic manifests foliation in large simple masses with rich sculpture on surfaces; late/declining Gothic multiplies foliation into lace-like subdivisions and relies on it to the detriment of mass and invention.
